https://www.dw.com/en/what-would-a-north.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ike8 North Korea's Kim Jong Un honored troops lost in the Ukraine war while opening a museum in April 2026 Image: KCNA/REUTERS Advertisement North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine , with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia , according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict. In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia. North Korea has suffered thousands of casualties in the Ukraine war Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later . Analysts believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region. Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded. This image, published by Ukrainian officials, shows North Korean soldiers being fitted for Russian uniforms Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front. Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality' South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer. Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country. "I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW. North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment. "Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military." Will North Koreans watch Russians' back? Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution. "Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW. "North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han. "Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine." Russian officials praise North Koreans "North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said. North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean casualties, some 2,000 may have been killed . "Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment ," Han said. "North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery." North Korean women also moving to Russia Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops." "North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979. "If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added. Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel." Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military." "However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn. "A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden." https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text: Experts have criticised the plan, saying the number of young people not in education, employment or training is likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remains high. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Experts have criticised the plan, saying the number of young people not in education, employment or training is likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remains high. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images Education Leaders attack ‘demotivating’ plan to make pupils who fail GCSEs retake maths and English Government announce plan for ‘stepping stone’ qualification as 620,000 year 11 students face retaking maths or English after failure to achieve grade 4 Richard Adams and Sally Weale Thu 20 Aug 2026 14.21 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The government’s plans to make young people continue studying maths and English if they fail GCSEs could be demotivating and ineffective, according to education experts and school leaders after retake pass rates slumped this year. Only one in seven students in the age group retaking GCSE maths after a previous failure got a grade 4 or above this summer, while only one in six managed to pass English, meaning the majority will have to retake the exams next year if they remain in education or training. The lower than expected results for older students came against a more positive national picture in which students in year 11 achieved record high grades in GCSE examinations across England. Compulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study finds Read more While seven in 10 of 16-year-olds achieved pass grades in maths and English, the remaining 620,000 year 11 students face retaking GCSE maths or English next year after failing to reach grade 4. Lucy Powell, the education secretary in England, said the government would be sticking with plans for a new “stepping stone” qualification aimed at those who got a grade 2 or worse in their first attempt at GCSEs. Powell described the current policy as “a hamster wheel” and said: “There’s got to be a better way to give young people the skills and confidence that they need to succeed, not just branding them a failure, and also allowing them to gain other qualifications that show they have a strong foundation in English and maths. “So that’s why I want to bring in a new level-one qualification so they’ve got a strong foundation in English and maths that gives them that passport to go on for further study or an apprenticeship or a training place.” But the plan, first announced in last year’s skills white paper, has been met with scepticism by experts and school leaders, who warned that the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) was likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remained high. Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “This year’s post-16 resit results reinforce the fact that the government policy of force-feeding them a relentless diet of GCSE English and maths in post-16 education is simply not working. “Tinkering at the edges of the qualification system will not solve this problem. As long as we continue to grade students in this way in these gateway subjects of English and maths, we will continue to damage their future prospects. “If the government is serious about tackling the Neet crisis it must grasp this nettle and rethink how we assess English and maths.” Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, warned that the new qualification would “need a strong fairness test to ensure this doesn’t create a two-tier system in which pupils from under-resourced backgrounds are disproportionately directed onto lower-level routes. “With around a third of young people not achieving the grade 4 benchmark in both English and maths, the system itself needs reform. This is the cruel injustice of narrow expectations: we need different pathways, but not different ceilings.” The Department for Education’s consultation positions the new “stepping stone” qualification as preparation for a later GCSE resit, meaning young people will still face multiple examinations while they remain in education. Paul Whiteman, head of the National Association of Head Teachers, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits. “What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.” GCSE results: almost one in four boys in England get top grades in maths Read more This year, the results revealed a strong performance in maths among boys in England, with a new high of 24% achieving grade 7 or above, while 20.5% of girls reached the same level. However, girls maintained their lead in top grades across all subjects, with 25.5% of their exam entries being awarded grade 7 or above compared with 20.7% of boys. The proportion of exam results at the top grade, 9, remained at 5.2%, unchanged from 2025. GCSEs in England award grades on a scale of 9 to 1, while many in Northern Ireland and Wales continue to award letter grades with A* at the peak. Education policy is devolved to UK national governments, making it difficult to directly compare GCSE results between them due to different content, marking and regulation. In Northern Ireland 31.5% of entries by 16-year-olds gained A or grade 7 and above, a slight improvement over last year, while 84.4% gained C or grade 4 and above. In Wales, 20.2% of grades for 16 year-olds were awarded A or better, and 63.7% of entries gained at least a C, slightly below the 2025 pass rate. Log in here » MIAMI (AP) — Prosecutors want social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in federal custody, arguing Monday that the brothers are a flight risk and a danger to the community, as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking. Three days after defense attorneys filed a motion for release, prosecutors filed their response in Miami federal court, where a hearing on Thursday will determine if the brothers should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. FILE - Andrew Tate, left, watches his brother Tristan speak, outside a police station in Voluntari, Romania, May 21, 2025. (AP Photo/Vadim Ghirda, File) The detention hearing is likely to be the first time the Tates leave the Federal Detention Center in Miami since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest. The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in the Tates’ long-running international legal saga spanning the U.S., Britain and Romania. Prosecutors claim a ‘heightened risk of flight’ According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office filing, the Tates should be detained pending their extradition hearing because they cannot overcome the strong presumption against bail in international extradition cases. The serious pending U.K. charges involving human trafficking and violent rapes and assaults against multiple victims, along with allegations in Romania that the Tates attempted to intimidate witnesses, present a clear public safety concern, prosecutors say. “That the Tates also claim to maintain multiple passports and identities, have access to excessive wealth and influence in numerous countries, and are stridently unwilling to voluntarily return to face prosecution in the United Kingdom, collectively demonstrate a heightened risk of flight that no amount of bond could overcome,” the filing says. The defense motion filed Friday acknowledges there is a presumption against bond in extradition proceedings but argues that release can be granted in special circumstances. It says the Tates’ high profile makes it nearly impossible for them to flee, and that they regularly post updates about their locations on social media. While prosecutors call the brothers a flight risk, their attorneys said they have proved they are not by complying with all pretrial restrictions in Romania, where they are accused of luring women for sexual exploitation. The U.K. has until mid-September to provide evidence to the State Department to support extradition, meaning the brothers could spend months in FDC Miami before the proceedings are resolved, the defense motion says. No date has been set for an extradition hearing. They are being held in a special unit for their own protection. Legal troubles follow the Tate brothers The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn’t moved forward due to legal and procedural problems. The Tates’ attorneys have said the Romanian court has granted a U.K. request for extradition that will take effect after Romanian proceedings conclude. Andrew Tate, 39, became famous a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was ejected from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. Tristan Tate, 38, has worked with his brother on multiple businesses, including the production of online webcam pornography. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-sets-its-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MMQl Royal Marine Commandos detained a sanctioned tanker, the Smyrtos, in the English Channel in June 2026 Image: LPhot Hutchins/Royal Navy/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport , it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions . But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities , including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions." Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party . In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table." Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea , but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong." Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel. Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior." In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations. Russia's threats: just a bluff? It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war." Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded. "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said. "Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels." After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through." Why did Norway seize a Russian ship for Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Armed Russian crews on board Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk. "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation." Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way. "It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel." Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Inspections would raise costs for Russia While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it." He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy." This article has been translated from German. What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast. https://nineoclock.ro/u-s-ambassador-dar.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount U.S. Ambassador to Romania Darryl Nirenberg marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks with a message honoring the victims and reflecting on the lasting impact of one of the darkest days in recent U.S. history. In a post published on his X account on September 11, Ambassador Nirenberg said that the anniversary is an opportunity to remember a day that “forever altered the course” of the United States’ history. “Today we reflect on the 25th anniversary of September 11, a day that forever altered the course of our nation’s history,” Nirenberg wrote. The ambassador also paid tribute to those who lost their lives in the attacks, emphasizing the importance of remembering their sacrifice and the values that continue to shape the legacy of September 11. “Together with the U.S. Embassy Bucharest community, we honor the memory of those who were killed, their sacrifice, and the enduring legacy of freedom they left behind,” he said. The September 11 attacks, carried out in 2001, claimed the lives of nearly 3,000 people and profoundly changed the United States, its foreign policy and the international security landscape. Twenty-five years later, memorial ceremonies and commemorations across the United States and around the world continue to honor the victims and remember the consequences of the attacks. Ambassador Nirenberg’s message also comes as the U.S. Embassy community in Bucharest joins Americans and communities worldwide in marking the anniversary and reflecting on the enduring importance of remembrance, freedom and solidarity. https://tradearabia.com:443/News/486529/.text: Energy, Oil & Gas MOL Group inaugurates 37.4 MWp solar park, energy storage system in Hungary Budapest/Algyő Sun, 20 Sep 2026 SHARE MOL Group has inaugurated a 37.4 MWp solar park and an associated battery energy storage system at its Algyő site in Hungary, strengthening the company’s renewable energy portfolio, energy independence and electricity supply flexibility. The storage system has 20 MW of nominal power and 40 MWh of capacity. Together, the new facilities are expected to reduce CO2 emissions by approximately 13,000 tonnes annually while helping manage fluctuations in renewable electricity generation. “Recent experience has highlighted the importance of managing intraday fluctuations in electricity generation. This is what we are achieving by commissioning our latest energy storage facility. The investment simultaneously promotes sustainability, security of supply and economic competitiveness: green electricity generated from our own sources reduces our reliance on external energy supplies, while the battery storage system contributes to the stability of the national power grid,” said György Bacsa, Group Chief Strategic Officer of MOL Group. The new solar park, combined with existing power plants at Algyő, can fully cover the electricity demand of MOL’s Algyő region. Its annual output is equivalent to the electricity consumption of around 22,500 households in Csongrád-Csanád County, where the facility is located. By replacing purchased electricity, the project is also expected to reduce operating costs and strengthen the site’s energy independence. The battery storage system will help balance electricity fluctuations caused by weather-dependent renewable sources. Its 40 MWh capacity is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 7,300 average households in the county. MOL said the project supports its long-term SHAPE TOMORROW strategy, under which expanding renewable generation and energy storage are key elements of its energy transition. The Algyő development is designed to support decarbonisation of the company’s operations while contributing to greater flexibility in Hungary’s electricity system. The solar park was constructed by ALTEO, which may also provide aggregation services following completion. MOL and its partners hold a 73.8% stake in ALTEO, which operates approximately 115 MW of renewable generation capacity from wind, solar, hydro and biogas facilities. MOL is continuing to expand its renewable energy portfolio across Central Europe. Following the Algyő project, the group operates nine solar parks in Hungary with combined capacity of 405 MW and two energy storage facilities with total capacity of 80 MWh. The company plans to increase its energy storage capacity in Hungary to 500 MWh by 2030. In Croatia, MOL operates two solar parks with combined capacity of 10 MW, with a third facility expected next year that will increase total capacity to 23 MW. With the newly inaugurated Algyő facilities, MOL Group’s total photovoltaic capacity across the region has reached 415 MWp, contributing to an estimated annual reduction of approximately 160,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions. -OGN /TradeArabia News Service Tags: MOL Group solar park energy storage system Hungary Related posts Russia eases diesel curbs; US releases 4m reserve barrels GAS Arabian Services lands Ghazlan 1 gas delivery system deal NESR, Aramco partner on region’s first direct lithium extraction project Saudi, UAE ink deal to boost power grid and rail links IMI, Lamprell partner on offshore structures manufacturing at Ras Al-Khair Khazna aims for 100% carbon-free electricity for cooling load by 2035 Utilities shift investment focus toward grid resilience, AI: IFS study TWMA secures multi-million-dollar North Sea drilling waste contract IEA members back faster oil stock releases amid market tightness Equinor, partners discover gas at Gullfaks South QatarEnergy wins seven exploration blocks in Brazil Bahrain calls for deeper GCC industrial integration to drive green growth Oil prices rise despite IEA accelerating the release of oil stocks Tarshid completes major energy efficiency retrofit project at Jazan University AMPO secures cryogenic valve contract for ADNOC’s Ruwais LNG project

Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters View image in fullscreen Christa Pike entering a Knox county criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on 4 December 2007. Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters Christa Pike Medical experts shocked by Tennessee team’s ‘malpractice’ in Christa Pike’s failed execution New details of IV team’s attempts to find a vein shared by Pike’s lawyer ‘shocked and disturbed’ practitioners Ed Pilkington in New York Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Medical experts have expressed shock at the apparent incompetence shown by Tennessee’s execution team during the failed lethal injection of Christa Pike , the prisoner who survived a normally fatal dose of pentobarbital, which they say would be considered medical malpractice in any other setting. New details emerged on Thursday of how Tennessee’s intravenous (IV) team struggled for almost an hour to set up a line into Pike’s arms through which she would be administered the fatal dose of sedative. A blow-by-blow account was released in legal proceedings from Pike’s lawyer, Randy Spivey, who was present inside the death chamber at her 30 September failed execution. The technical procedures attempted by the four unidentified members of the IV team as they tried to find a vein, as described by Spivey , provoked alarm among medical experts. They said the standards applied appeared to fall glaringly short of anything that would be deemed acceptable in a medical environment. Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution Read more “I’m shocked and disturbed by what happened inside the death chamber,” said Jonathan Groner, emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University and an expert in execution methods. “The level of incompetence is astounding, and difficult to comprehend.” Groner, who has written an upcoming book The Hippocratic Paradox that explores the ethical contradictions involved in lethal injections, said that Spivey’s detailed chronology painted a picture in which nobody was in charge and there was no plan in sight. “What they did to Christa Pike would have been malpractice in a clinical situation. Nobody would infuse a drug like pentobarbital that’s known to cause burns if they were unsure that the IV was actually in place.” Groner pointed out that the label on a vial of pentobarbital instructs that infusion should cease immediately if the patient complains of pain. Spivey’s account records multiple times in which Pike “grimaced” and said her arm was “really burning”. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. Following the failed execution, she spent several days on a ventilator and her lawyers assumed she was brain-dead. After 10 days in hospital she was returned to her prison cell. She can now talk and walk, but her long-term prospects are not known. The gruesome nature of Pike’s experiences in the death chamber, which some have likened to torture, have prompted a reckoning on the death penalty nationwide. Tennessee has called off all executions, pending a review. In Spivey’s detailed account, the IV team used about 10 needles as they repeatedly poked Pike’s arms, failing to secure a line. At several points, team members worried that her veins might have “blown”. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, who gave expert testimony at legal hearings ahead of Pike’s failed execution, said that the new chronology pointed to several areas of serious concern. “Here we have a poorly written protocol, no one in charge, technology that they may not have had permission to use, and catheters that are far too small for the purpose. We could go on and on …” Pike’s lawyers, partly on the basis of Zivot’s expert opinion, warned the state on several occasions before the failed execution attempt that the prisoner had exceptionally small and compromised veins. The Spivey timeline records that at 7.05pm on the evening of the failed execution, about half an hour into the procedure, a member of the IV team asked for a 24-gauge needle “and moved that needle around a lot. Christa continued to grimace.” Zivot said that a 24-gauge catheter was very small. “That’s the kind of catheter you put in a baby, or a small child.” He added there was “no way that you can push a 50cc syringe into that small little catheter without it blowing up the vein”. Under Tennessee’s protocol, 50cc of pentobarbital were to be injected into each of Pike’s arms, giving a massive total dose of 5g of the sedative. At 7.07pm another member of the IV team said: “I think it is blown.” The Spivey chronology also reveals that the IV team attempted to find a vein using ultrasound technology. Groner said that from his own personal experience using an ultrasound requires many hours of specialist training and up to 20 actual procedures before an individual can perform the technique smoothly. “Inserting an IV with ultrasound guidance is a practice-based skill that takes a lot of training. The Tennessee team clearly didn’t know how to use it,” he said. At 7.23pm in the timeline, the IV team pushed saline through the line they had established “with difficulty”, according to Spivey. That should have been a flashing red light, Groner said. “No clinician would give a caustic drug through an IV where it didn’t flush easily. That would be malpractice.” Despite that warning sign, the IV team concluded that the IV was set and that the procedure could commence just a minute later, at 7.24pm. The medical experts said the timeline underlined fundamental problems with lethal injections, the overwhelmingly dominant form of executions in the US in the modern era. Groner said that it highlighted that lethal injections were a “medical charade. Pike didn’t deserve this. The ultimate penalty in our country, whether one agrees with it or not, is death. It is not torture, then death.” Zivot said his takeaway was that the execution team pressed on when they should have stopped. “It was clear this was not doable, and yet they kept on doing it anyway.” He added: “Lethal injection is a theft of a medical procedure, and they stole the wrong part. Medicine is obsessed with safety, accountability and training. You didn’t see any of those things in Pike’s execution chamber.” Explore more on these topics Christa Pike Tennessee Capital punishment news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
